doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Barry Harris, This Here and Nat Adderley's chase
summary: Bobby Timmons left for Blakey; Barry Harris parodied This Here until Nat Adderley chased him down the street.

bands.name: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: You had a small anecdote, I don’t know if you want to mention the person’s name again, that you said something about Nat chasing some piano player down the street.

Oh no that’s a lovely story. Bobby Timmons was of course the Adderley’s, this band’s first piano player. And Cannon had been kind of a little unhappy about circumstances, he really wanted to have Bobby in the band but it meant in effect stealing him away from Art Blakey, you know the year before Bobby had wrote “Moanin’” which had been a great hit for Blakey, and after a while Bobby for one reason or another decided to go back to Blakey. And Cannon’s idea of filling the vacant chair was this really wonderful young piano player in Detroit that he was aware of, musicians were very aware of, that hadn’t been on the scene, Barry Harris. And one of the reasons that Cannonball hired Barry was because there was a degree of musical erudition and a melodic quality to Barry and Cannon was kind of concerned, he didn’t want the band to become like known as nothing but a funk band, and nothing but the band that plays “This Here.” So he brought Barry in partially to emphasize a more melodic side of the band, but very early in Barry’s regime there is this incessant demand for “This Here” that it gets played every set because that’s what the audience is looking for and that’s what’s getting all the airplay. And it’s not Barry Harris’ kind of music. Barry was pretty unhappy having to consistently play that tune. And basically Barry always has been a pretty good team player and he wasn’t hollering too much about it, but he was uncomfortable and after a while it begins to get you down. And what he started to do was kind of to Burlesque the tune a little bit, to make fun of it somewhat, to play it more and more broadly. As he once said I think he was going to play it the way Jelly Roll Morton would have played it. I mean as long as we’re doing this kind of thing, you know, so that it got to be noticeable that he was doing pretty much of a parody version of it. And Nat Adderley, who in addition to being the younger brother, really was the guy that took care of business and took care of paying people and was pretty much the straw boss of the band, and he felt that if band discipline was his problem, Cannonball was too easygoing anyhow. So quite a thing developed between him and Barry about his wanting Barry to stop playing the tune that way and Barry in effect feeling it was the only way he could preserve his sanity, it was the only way he could give himself some relief from having to play this damn thing all the time. And it just came to a head one night, actually it was during a return engagement at the Jazz Workshop, which probably made the whole thing worse and Barry just played the screwed up version of “This Here” once too often as far as Nat was concerned, and what happened was really there was a big shouting match going on and a guy going after a guy and Barry was out the front door and running down the street with Nat running after him. He finally gave up, didn’t catch up with him, don’t know what he would have done if he
did, and actually that relieved the tension a lot. But it’s a story worth remembering. I don’t think Barry will object to it, and I understand exactly what he was doing.
